findings.issue: The ASCII \b anchor rejects a key whenever the preceding character is a letter, digit or underscore, so keys that the old patterns redacted now pass through: percent-encoded contexts (`?api_key%3Dsk-…`, `%2Fghp_…`, `%20ghp_…`, `%22sk-…`), a literal escaped newline or tab in pasted JSON/log text (`\nghp_…`, `\tsk-…`), and underscore-joined or emphasised text (`OPENAI_API_KEY_sk-…`, `_ghp_…_`). The catch-all token/secret/password/api_key pattern covers none of these.
findings.consequence: A real GitHub or OpenAI key in those shapes, in a PR body, review comment or session excerpt, reaches the committed review, evidence and learning Markdown unredacted, a regression against the pre-change patterns. A guard that excludes only a preceding lowercase letter, allowing an escape sequence, keeps #184's fix while redacting these.

findings.issue: TestRedactLeavesWordsThatContainKeyPrefixes does not pin the new anchor on the github_pat_ pattern: no keep case has github_pat_ inside a word and no secret case is a github_pat_ token. With the anchor removed from github_pat_ only, the test still passes.
findings.consequence: If the github_pat_ anchor were removed, or the pattern stopped matching real fine-grained PATs, the test would not catch it.

findings.issue: The guard `(?:^|[^a-z]|\\[nrt])` rejects any key directly after a lowercase letter, which includes the last digit of lowercase-hex percent-encoding and other backslash escapes: `%2fghp_ABCDEFGH12345678`, `%3dsk-proj-abcdefghijklmnopqrstuv`, `x%3aghs_ABCDEFGH1234` and `\bghp_…` all pass through Redact unchanged, though the unguarded patterns redacted them before this diff. The comment claims percent-encoding is covered, but only uppercase hex is.
findings.consequence: A real GitHub or OpenAI token in a URL using lowercase hex (a pasted `?next=%2fghp_…` or `token%3dsk-…` link in a PR body or comment) now leaks into the review context.

findings.issue: Redact now runs redactKeyPrefixes before secretPatterns, reversing the old order where the Authorization: Bearer pattern ran first. Once a key prefix has turned the start of a bearer token into '[REDACTED]', the bearer pattern no longer matches ('[' is not in its class), so any part of the token outside the key charset ('.', '~', '+', '/', '=') is left in the output, e.g. 'Authorization: Bearer sk-abcdefghijklmnopqrstuv.SECRETTAIL' → 'Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED].SECRETTAIL'; a lowercase 'authorization: bearer ghp_…' is also no longer normalised.
findings.consequence: A bearer token that starts with a provider prefix and continues past the key charset has its tail printed in the rendered GitHub context, a regression against the previous ordering. Running the Authorization pattern (or all secretPatterns) before redactKeyPrefixes restores it.

findings.issue: No secret case asserts that the guard character survives redaction. Changing `text[last:m[2]]` to `text[last:m[0]]` in redactKeyPrefixes, which drops the guard character, still passes the test.
findings.consequence: A regression that eats the preceding character ('=', '(', a space, half of a \n escape) goes unnoticed and corrupts the text around each redaction, e.g. '(ghs_…)' becomes '[REDACTED])'.

findings.issue: The literal \r escape alternative in keyGuard is never tested; changing `\\[nrt]` to `\\[nt]` still passes.
findings.consequence: A key right after a literal \r escape in pasted JSON or log text could stop being redacted with no failing test.

findings.issue: keyGuard treats every preceding lowercase letter as a word interior, but common machine-generated contexts end in a lowercase letter directly before a key: ANSI SGR colour codes (ESC[32m, ESC[0m, and the JSON-escaped \u001b[1m), multi-character escapes such as \x3d, and JSON unicode escapes left literal (\u003c, \u003e, \u0026, \u003d). `\x1b[32mghp_ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOP`, `\x3dghp_…` and `\u003cghp_…` all pass through Redact unchanged; the original unguarded patterns redacted them.
findings.consequence: A real key printed in colour in terminal or CI output (session transcripts pass through sessionhistory's Redact, pasted CI logs through githubcontext) or after a hex/unicode escape in double-escaped JSON reaches committed review and learning artifacts in full. Enumerating allowed contexts keeps missing shapes.

findings.issue: No test puts an uppercase letter or a digit directly before a key, so narrowing the guard's [^a-z] to [^A-Za-z] or [^a-z0-9] passes the whole suite, although the comment promises redaction after both.
findings.consequence: A later tightening that stops redacting keys after an uppercase letter or digit ('KEYghp_…', '0sk-…' in concatenated or base64-adjacent text) would pass CI and leak.

output.summary: Replaced the context-enumerating guard with a per-match predicate: skip only lowercase-only, word-interior matches. Real (uppercase-bearing) keys redact after ANSI, \x, \u escapes or letters; tests cover these plus uppercase/digit contexts; each predicate branch mutation-pinned.

findings.issue: The doc comment on TestRedactKeepsTheCharacterBeforeAKey says the character in front of the key is 'the guard the pattern consumes', which described an earlier iteration; the final code uses unanchored keyPrefixPatterns and a keyIsWordInterior post-filter, so no pattern consumes a guard character.
findings.consequence: A maintainer could believe the regexes carry a leading guard group and adjust offsets wrongly; documentation drift only.

findings.issue: The index-bounds guards in keyIsWordInterior are not pinned: mutating `start >= 2` to `start >= 1` and `start >= 3` to `start >= 2` passes the suite, because no keep-case has a lowercase-only match at offset 1 or 2 after a lowercase letter (e.g. "xsk-abcdefghijklmnopqrstu", "xyghp_abcdefghijkl").
findings.consequence: If the guards are later loosened, Redact panics with an index out of range on short lowercase inputs, and Redact runs over every review log and GitHub context, so the panic would take down the gate.

findings.issue: The range of the uppercase scan is not pinned: mutating text[start:end] to text[start:] or text[start:end-1] passes every test, since no keep-case has an uppercase letter after the word-interior match and no secret case has its only uppercase letter last; the 'A'/'Z' and 'z' range endpoints are also untested.

findings.issue: No test has a skipped word-interior match followed by a real key for the same pattern in one string, so nothing checks that redactKeyPrefixes keeps scanning after a skip: changing its `continue` to `break` passes the whole suite, and then Redact("see task-done-abcdefghijklmnopqrstu then sk-abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123") returns the key unredacted.
findings.consequence: A regression that stops the scan after the first word-interior skip would ship green and leak every later sk-/gh*_ key in any text that first mentions a task-done path, which review logs routinely do.

findings.issue: The test's header comment says the sk- and gh*_ patterns "must not start inside a word", left over from the \b design; the implementation and the test itself redact word-interior matches that contain an uppercase letter.
findings.consequence: A reader could 'fix' the code to match the comment and stop redacting real keys that follow a letter (after ANSI codes or \x3d escapes). Documentation only.

findings.consequence: The comment misstates which keyIsWordInterior branch those cases exercise, which could mislead someone changing the escape handling. Documentation only.

output.summary: Two cases combine a skipped word-interior match with a later real key (continue->break mutation now caught); stale test comments and the long doc line fixed.

findings.issue: keyIsWordInterior assumes every real key has an uppercase letter, but some providers issue all-lowercase hex sk- keys (e.g. DeepSeek: sk- + 32 lowercase hex). Such a key glued to a lowercase word (`mykeysk-0123abcd…`) is no longer redacted.
findings.consequence: A narrow leak for all-lowercase hex keys directly after a lowercase letter; a hex-only body is not word-like text and could be treated as a key.

findings.issue: #184's AC3 (a newly generated pr-ready log lists task-done evidence paths that resolve) is covered only at the Redact unit level; no internal/prready test renders the evidence review line through evidence.go's Redact call and checks the path survives.
findings.consequence: If the prready line format or redaction routing changes, rendered pr-ready logs could produce unresolvable '[REDACTED]' paths again with no failing test.

findings.issue: The doc comment says keyIsWordInterior excludes a lowercase byte that ends a %XX percent-escape, but the code checks only text[start-3]=='%' and isHexASCII(text[start-2]), not that text[start-1] is hex, so '%2g' or '%1z' also count as escapes.
findings.consequence: Comment and code disagree slightly (on the safe side: extra redaction, no leak), which could mislead a maintainer.

findings.issue: The group commented as lowercase-hex percent-escape cases includes '?next=%2fghp_ABCDEFGH12345678' and 'x%3aghs_ABCDEFGH1234abcdefghijklmnop', which contain uppercase letters and are redacted by the uppercase rule before the %XX branch runs; only 'token%3dsk-proj-…' exercises the percent exception (same at the exact-output case).
findings.consequence: The comment overstates coverage of the percent-escape rule; if the one real case changes, that branch loses coverage unnoticed.

findings.issue: #184 proposes `\bsk-`; the implementation uses a different rule (skip only lowercase-only, word-interior matches), deliberately leaving a lowercase-only key glued to a lowercase word unredacted. The code documents the trade-off but the issue does not record the deviation, and AC3 is not shown end to end.
findings.consequence: The scope change and the end-to-end criterion should be recorded on #184 or in the PR so reviewers see the accepted trade-off.
